gold: Organized thrombus formation on native bicuspid aortic valve with ascending aortic aneurysm
e7_s4_rationale: The presence of a bicuspid aortic valve with mild aortic regurgitation, along with an ascending aortic aneurysm and an organized thrombus at the left coronary cusp, points towards a complex condition that involves both the aortic valve and the aorta. Bicuspid aortic valve disease is known to be associated with aortic aneurysms and can lead to complications such as aortic regurgitation and thrombus

e7_s4_rejected.label: Aortic aneurysm
e7_s4_rejected.why: While an ascending aortic aneurysm is present, it is not the primary diagnosis that explains all key facts, including the bicuspid aortic valve and thrombus formation.

e7_s4_rejected.label: Aortic valve endocarditis
e7_s4_rejected.why: There is no clear evidence of infection or inflammation that would suggest endocarditis, and the histopathological examination confirmed the excised mass as an organized thrombus without mention of infectious agents.

e7_s4_rejected.label: Coronary artery thrombosis
e7_s4_rejected.why: The primary issue is not with the coronary arteries themselves but with the thrombus formation at the left coronary cusp of the aortic valve, which affects blood perfusion in the left coronary artery.

e7_s4_rejected.label: Marfan syndrome
e7_s4_rejected.why: There is no mention of systemic features or family history that would suggest Marfan syndrome, which typically involves multiple systems including the skeletal, ocular, and cardiovascular systems beyond just the aortic root dilatation and aortic valve issues.
